title: AI Ethics, Safety & Fairness
html:
AI systems make or influence decisions about loans, jobs, medical care and what people see. Building them responsibly means asking not only does it work? but for whom, with what failures, and who is accountable?

Core principles

Fairness

Outcomes shouldn't systematically disadvantage groups defined by race, gender, age, disability…

Transparency & explainability

People affected should know AI is used and get understandable reasons for decisions.

Privacy

Data is collected with consent, minimised and protected; models shouldn't leak training data.

Safety & robustness

Systems behave reliably under distribution shift, adversarial inputs and misuse.

Accountability

A human or organisation is answerable for the system's decisions; there are audit trails and appeals.

Human oversight

Humans can monitor, override or switch off the system, especially in high-stakes uses.

Where bias comes from

SourceExample
Historical biasPast hiring data reflects past discrimination; a model trained on it reproduces it
Representation / sampling biasFace datasets with few darker-skinned faces → higher error rates for those groups
Measurement biasUsing arrests as a proxy for crime, or health spending as a proxy for health need
Proxy featuresRemoving “race” doesn't help if postcode or name still encodes it
Feedback loopsPredictive policing sends officers where arrests were recorded, generating more records there

Measuring fairness

CriterionRequires equal across groupsIntuition
Demographic paritySelection rate P(ŷ = 1)Same share of each group approved
Equal opportunityTrue-positive rate P(ŷ = 1 | y = 1)Qualified people approved equally often
Equalised oddsTPR and false-positive rateEqual error rates of both kinds
Predictive parity / calibrationP(y = 1 | ŷ = 1) or scores mean the sameAn approval means the same thing for everyone
Watch out

These criteria cannot all hold at once when base rates differ between groups (the impossibility results of Kleinberg et al. and Chouldechova, 2016–17). Choosing a fairness metric is a value judgement about the application, not a purely technical choice.

Safety and alignment

RiskWhat it looks likeMitigation
Specification gaming / reward hackingThe system optimises the literal objective, not the intent (see Reinforcement Learning)Careful objectives, human feedback, red-teaming
Distribution shiftA model trained on one hospital's scans fails at anotherMonitoring, robust evaluation, domain adaptation
Adversarial examplesTiny pixel changes flip a classifier; prompt injection hijacks an LLM agentAdversarial training, input validation, least-privilege tools
Hallucination / overconfidenceFluent but false answersRetrieval grounding, calibrated uncertainty, citations, human review
MisuseDeepfakes, fraud, disinformation, cyber-attacksUsage policies, watermarking, access controls
Alignment of capable systemsGoals that diverge from human values; hard to correct once deployedInterpretability, scalable oversight, evaluations before release

Governance

FrameworkKey idea
EU AI Act (in force 2024, phased in to 2026–27)Risk tiers: unacceptable (banned, e.g. social scoring), high-risk (hiring, credit, medical — strict obligations), limited (transparency, e.g. chatbots must disclose), minimal; extra duties for general-purpose models
NIST AI Risk Management Framework (2023)Voluntary US framework: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage
OECD / UNESCO AI principlesInternational baselines for trustworthy, human-centred AI
Model cards & datasheetsDocumentation of intended use, training data, evaluation by subgroup and limitations
Do

Evaluate performance per subgroup, document data and limits, keep a human in the loop for high-stakes decisions, and monitor after deployment.

Avoid

Assume a model is fair because the protected attribute was dropped, or ship without a way to appeal or override its decisions.

The Machine Learning notes' Responsible AI & Ethics topic covers the practical checklist for ML projects in more depth.

How can a model be biased if it never sees the protected attribute?

Other features act as proxies (postcode, name, school), and the labels themselves may encode historical discrimination. Fairness must be measured on outcomes per group, not assumed from the input list.

What is the alignment problem?

Making sure an AI system pursues the goals its designers and users actually intend, including unstated constraints — rather than a literal proxy objective. It grows harder as systems become more capable and autonomous.

Name two fairness metrics and explain why they can conflict.

Demographic parity (equal approval rates) and equal opportunity (equal true-positive rates). If qualified-applicant base rates differ between groups, a perfectly accurate model satisfies equal opportunity but violates demographic parity; forcing parity then changes error rates for some group.
